lessons.title: How Sales, Procurement and Operations Decisions Lock Up Working Capital

children.text: Nobody in a company sets out to lock up cash. The sales head wins an order. The purchase manager negotiates a discount. The plant head hits his utilisation target. The marketing team launches a product. Every one of these is somebody doing their job well, and every one of them moves money into inventory or receivables.

This lesson is for everyone outside finance. It maps the everyday decisions each function makes to the working capital lines they move, and gives you the one question that turns a commercial instinct into a commercial decision.

Take a manufacturer with ₹200 crore of sales and ₹140 crore of cost of goods sold. One day of sales is about ₹0.55 crore, and one day of cost is about ₹0.38 crore. Now watch four ordinary decisions taken in the same year.

body.caption: What each decision costs in cash (₹ crore)

cells: Sales
Offers 60-day terms instead of 45 to win volume
Receivables
Procurement
Bulk buys six months of a key input for a 1% discount
Inventory
Operations
Runs longer batches to hit a plant utilisation target
Inventory

Inventory

body.title: Cash locked up by each decision (₹ crore)

stats.label: Total cash locked up
stats.context: From four decisions nobody thought of as financial

stats.label: Where it was decided
stats.context: None of them the finance department

body.text: Notice that none of these decisions was wrong on its own terms. The sales team did win volume. The purchase manager did get a discount. The problem is that each was evaluated on its own measure, and the cash consequence landed on a balance sheet nobody in those rooms was looking at.

children.text: Some of These Trades Actually Pay
The point is not that locking up cash is bad. It is that the trade has to be computed. Look at the same four decisions with their benefits included.

body.caption: Benefit against carrying cost (₹ crore a year)
headers: Carrying cost of the cash locked up

cells: Sales: 60-day terms instead of 45
Volume, not quantified
Unknown, because nobody costed the volume gain
Procurement: 1% discount on ₹60 crore of bulk buying
Operations: fewer changeovers
Marketing: four new variants
Range, not quantified
Unknown, because no contribution target was set

children.text: The procurement decision is genuinely positive: a ₹0.6 crore discount against ₹0.46 crore of carrying cost, a net gain of ₹0.14 crore. The operations decision is marginal at ₹0.04 crore, which means it comes down to whether the stock actually sells. The other two are unknown, not because they are bad, but because nobody quantified the benefit against the cost.

body.text: Beware the discount that is smaller than the carrying cost. A 1% discount for holding six months of stock is roughly a 2% annualised return on the money tied up, which is far below any Indian cost of funds. Procurement teams win these negotiations and lose the arithmetic routinely.

body.title: Price a credit decision
body.prompt: A company with ₹320 crore of annual sales agrees to extend credit terms across its dealer network by 12 days. How much additional cash does that lock up in receivables, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: One day of sales is ₹320 crore divided by 365, about ₹0.88 crore. Twelve days locks up roughly ₹10.52 crore, permanently, for as long as the terms stay in place. At a 10% cost of funds that is about ₹1.05 crore a year, which is the number the decision should have been weighed against.

cells: Sales
Longer credit terms, quarter-end pushes, accepting slow-paying customers, wide product range
Advance payment terms, collection discipline, discounting for early payment, customer rationalisation
Marketing
New variants needing pipeline stock, promotional stock builds, packaging redesigns that obsolete existing stock
Retiring slow variants, planning launches with phased stock builds
Procurement
Bulk buying, high minimum order quantities, advance payments to secure supply, imports with long lead times
Negotiating longer supplier terms, splitting orders, developing local second sources
Operations
Long production runs, high safety stock, rework and rejections, long lead times
Shorter changeovers, better yield, faster throughput, disciplined reorder levels
Finance
Poor forecasting that forces buffers everywhere, slow invoicing
Accurate invoicing, structured collections, matched funding
Human resources
Lump-sum bonus and increment timing, headcount growth ahead of revenue
Staggered payouts, incentive schemes tied to cash rather than to booked orders

children.text: That last row is quieter than the others and worth a moment. If annual bonuses of ₹4 crore are paid in one month, that is roughly 7.27 days of sales leaving the business on a single date. It does not change annual working capital, but it can absolutely break a month, particularly if it lands in the same quarter as an advance tax instalment.
You cannot fix working capital by explaining it. It is fixed by changing what each function is measured on, because people optimise what is on their scorecard.

body.title: Two versions of the same scorecard

columns.label: What usually gets measured
points: Sales: orders booked and revenue recognised
Procurement: price per unit and discounts negotiated
Operations: plant utilisation and output volume
Marketing: range breadth and launch count
Result: four functions optimising four numbers, none of which is cash

columns.label: What should sit alongside it
points: Sales: cash collected, days sales outstanding, and the value over 90 days
Procurement: landed cost after carrying cost, plus supplier payment terms achieved
Operations: inventory days and on time in full delivery, read together
Marketing: contribution per variant, with a retirement rule for slow ones
Result: the cash consequence sits with the person who caused it

body.text: The single highest-return change most Indian companies can make is to pay sales incentives on collection rather than on booking. It costs nothing to implement, it changes behaviour within one quarter, and it removes the incentive to sell to customers who will not pay.

body.title: The quarter-end push, and why it is a working capital problem

children.text: Near a quarter end, sales teams under pressure push stock into the distribution channel beyond what it can sell. Revenue is recognised, targets are met, and the balance sheet absorbs the consequence: receivables rise, the distributor slows payment because the stock has not moved, and the following quarter opens with a weak order book.

, and it shows up in exactly the pattern Chapter 2 taught you to look for: receivable days rising faster than sales, with a seasonal spike at each quarter end. From inside the company, the tell is a sharp rise in dispatches in the last ten days of a quarter followed by a collapse in the first two weeks of the next one.

markDefs.definition: Pushing more stock onto distributors near a period end than they can sell, which books revenue now and returns as receivables pressure later.

children.text: It is treated more fully in the next lesson but two, as a red flag when you are analysing someone else's company. Here the point is narrower: if your own incentive structure rewards booking rather than collection, you are paying people to create this pattern.

body.title: Who should own inventory days?
body.question: A company wants to assign clear ownership for inventory days as a metric. Which arrangement is most likely to work?
options: Finance, since it prepares the balance sheet where inventory appears
Operations and procurement jointly, with finance reporting the number and service levels reported alongside it
The managing director, since it cuts across functions
Nobody, since inventory is driven by customer demand and cannot be controlled
body.explanation: Inventory is created by ordering and production decisions, so ownership belongs with the people who make them. Finance should report the number rather than own it, and the service measure must be reported alongside, or the metric will simply be met by starving the business of stock.

body.title: The one question to ask
body.textWithBlank: Before agreeing to longer credit, bigger stock or an advance payment, the question that turns an instinct into a decision is: how much ___ does this lock up, and for how long?
body.explanation: Converting a commercial decision into days and then into rupees takes about a minute with the daily sales figure, and it is the habit that separates a costed decision from a hopeful one.

body.title: The argument in the monthly meeting
body.scenario: The sales head has won a ₹30 crore annual contract with a large retail chain at 90-day terms, against the company standard of 45. Contribution margin is 22%. The finance head objects that the company's cash credit limit is already 80% drawn and the business funds itself at 10.5%. The sales head replies that the contract is the biggest win in three years and that finance is blocking growth. Annual sales are ₹200 crore.
body.prompt: How would you resolve this in the meeting, using numbers rather than positions?
body.modelAnswer:
Convert both arguments into the same units before anyone repeats themselves.

The contract adds ₹30 crore of sales at 22% contribution, which is ₹6.6 crore a year. The receivables it creates are ₹30 crore times 90 divided by 365, about ₹7.4 crore, against ₹3.7 crore if it were on standard 45-day terms. So the extra funding attributable to the longer terms is roughly ₹3.7 crore, costing about ₹0.39 crore a year at 10.5%. Against ₹6.6 crore of contribution, that is comfortably worth doing on profit alone.

So the sales head is right about the economics, and the finance head is right about something else entirely: the company does not have ₹7.4 crore of headroom. Eighty per cent drawn on the limit means the constraint is availability of cash, not profitability of the contract. These are different objections and the meeting is conflating them.

What to decide. Accept the contract and fund it deliberately. Check first whether the retail chain is registered on a TReDS platform, since a large listed buyer usually is, and discounting those invoices would convert the 90-day exposure into cash in days at a rate below the company's own. If not, take the incremental funding request to the bank with this arithmetic attached, because a ₹6.6 crore contribution against a ₹3.7 crore funding need is an easy credit conversation. And set the internal rule now: any terms beyond 45 days require this calculation and a named funding source before the offer is made, not after it is accepted.

body.label: The conversion everyone should know
body.context: Annual sales divided by 365. At ₹200 crore that is ₹0.55 crore. Any change in credit terms or stock cover multiplied by this number turns a policy discussion into a cash number in about ten seconds.

body.title: Run a working capital review that actually changes behaviour
steps: Hold it monthly, with sales, procurement, operations, marketing and finance in the same room.
Open with three numbers: inventory days, receivable days and payable days, each against last month and last year.
Assign one named owner to each of the three lines, and never let finance own all three.
Report a service measure alongside the inventory number, so nobody wins by starving the business of stock.
Review the oldest receivables and the slowest-moving stock by name, not as totals.
Convert every proposed change in terms or stock cover into rupees before deciding it.
Check that incentive schemes reward collection and contribution rather than booking and volume.
Track one improvement action per function to closure, rather than discussing the same numbers again next month.

body.text: Working capital is not created in the finance department. It is created in a hundred ordinary decisions taken by people who were never shown what those decisions cost, and it is fixed by changing what those people are measured on.

points: Sales, procurement, operations, marketing and human resources all move working capital through decisions that are rarely seen as financial.
In the worked example, four routine decisions locked up ₹17.81 crore and cost ₹1.78 crore a year to carry.
Locking up cash is not automatically wrong, but the trade has to be computed: benefit against carrying cost.
A 1% discount for six months of extra stock is roughly a 2% annualised return, far below any Indian cost of funds.
Lump-sum bonus timing and headcount decisions make human resources a working capital function too.
Behaviour follows the scorecard, so pay sales incentives on collection rather than on booking.
Give each working capital line a named owner outside finance, and always report inventory alongside a service measure.
